He pushed open the door so quietly that the old hinges gave only the faintest sigh of complaint. The room was sinking into a grey twilight, and for a moment he could not see her. Then a small, frustrated sound from the corner by the window drew his eye. His grandmother sat there, her head bent low over her work.

"What troubles you, Elspeth?" he said, his voice soft in the still air.

She started, letting her hands fall into her lap. "Oh, Silas! I did not hear you come in. 'Tis nothing, child, only this vexing thread." She held up the needle, a glint of steel in the gloom. "The eye of it plays tricks on me to-day."

He walked over and knelt by her chair, taking her worn, trembling hand in his own. "Let me."

"No, no," she said, shaking her head, though she made no move to pull her hand away. "I have done it a thousand times, ten thousand. I can do it again. 'Tis only the poor light."

"The light has been poor for a long while now, grandmother," he said gently. "And you have watched and worked in it long enough."

"What else is there for me to do?" she cried, her voice suddenly cracking with a sorrow she could no longer hold back. "My eyes are no good for the fields, and soon they'll be no good for this, neither! And then what shall I be, Silas? Just a mouth to feed and a chair to sit in! O, that the good Lord would just let me be useful 'till the end!"

He took the needle and thread from her fingers without a word. He did not need to look closely; his young eyes found the opening at once, and he pushed the thread through with a steady hand. He gave it back to her. She took it, her admiration warring with her sadness.

"You have your father's hands, so quick and sure," she murmured, wiping at a tear with the back of her other hand. "He was always a comfort to me, and so are you."

"Then let me be a comfort now," Silas said, rising to his feet but staying close by her side. He looked around the small, bare room; its emptiness seemed to echo the hollowness in his own purse. "I have been thinking, Elspeth."

"What about, dear?"

"About the city. Mr. Albright has need of a clerk in his shipping office. He says the pay is steady."

She looked up at him, her face full of alarm. "The city? Mannahatta? Oh, Silas, that is no place for you! 'Tis a wilderness of brick and noise, not like here. You would not have the clean air, or the quiet."

"Nor would you," he answered, his meaning clear.

"Me?" Her voice was a whisper. "You mean to take me with you?"

"I cannot leave you here," he said simply. "I cannot be at peace, thinking of you struggling with the fire and the mending and the dim light. 'Tis not right."

"But your own life, child! You will be tied to an old woman."

"You are the root from which I grew, Elspeth," he said, laying a hand upon her shoulder. "The tree does not complain that it is tied to the ground. It is where it belongs." He felt a tremor go through her, a quiet surrender. "Would you rather I stay?"

"No," she said, her voice faint but firm. "No, Silas. If you must go, I will go too. I could not bear the quiet here, if you were gone."

And Winthrop did. The words came out in a halting, broken flood. He spoke of the farm, of the mortgage taken out for his and Rufus's advancement, of his father's toil and his mother's sorrow. He told of the five years of unpaid interest, of Mr. Haye's impatience, and of the threat of foreclosure by the summer's end. He laid bare the whole story of his family's long, quiet struggle with poverty, a story he had guarded so jealously. As he spoke, he kept his eyes fixed on the floor, unable to meet his benefactor's gaze, feeling the full weight of his humiliation.
"I received a letter from my father yesterday," he concluded, his voice sinking almost to a whisper. "He sees no way out but to sell, and go to the West. And I... the money I earn, which seemed so much to me, is nothing against such a debt. I cannot help them. I have failed them."
There was a long silence after he had finished. The only sound in the room was the ticking of the tall clock in the corner. Winthrop braced himself for the response: for pity, perhaps; or for a kind but firm refusal; or worse, a lecture on imprudence. He felt stripped bare, his pride in tatters.
At last, Mr. Thorne spoke, his voice grave but devoid of any judgment. "And what is the sum required to satisfy this Mr. Haye?"
Winthrop told him. The amount sounded enormous, even to his own ears, in this room of quiet wealth.
Mr. Thorne nodded slowly. He rose from his desk and walked to the window, his hands clasped behind his back. He stood there for some time, looking out into the square. Winthrop waited, his hands clenched together in his lap, his anxiety a physical sickness.
Finally, Mr. Thorne turned back to him. His face was serious, but Winthrop saw in it not a trace of the pity or condescension he had feared. He saw only a deep, thoughtful compassion.
"Winthrop," he said, returning to his chair. "There are two kinds of wilderness in this world. There is the wilderness of the West, with its forests and its prairies. And there is the wilderness of a man's own soul when he is beset by troubles he cannot master. It seems you are caught between the two."
He paused, then leaned forward, his eyes meeting Winthrop's directly. "I will help you," he said simply.
The relief was so immense, so sudden, that Winthrop felt dizzy. Tears he had been holding back sprang to his eyes, and he could not speak.
"However," Mr. Thorne continued, holding up a hand, "we will not do this as a gift. A gift would wound you, and it would create a false relationship between us. I have not invested in you, my boy, to make you a dependent. I have invested in you because I believe you are a man of character and talent, who will one day do great things. We will treat this as a matter of business."
Winthrop looked at him, confused, hope and apprehension mingling in his heart.
"I will advance you the full amount of the mortgage," said Mr. Thorne, his tone becoming brisk and practical. "It will be a loan, from me to you. Not to your father. To you. I will draw up a note of hand, at a low rate of interest, much lower than your Mr. Haye would dream of. The principal will be due to me, in ten years. It can be repaid from your future earnings. Your work for me, and for others, will in time be more than sufficient. This way, the farm is saved, your father is freed from his obligation to Mr. Haye, and you, Winthrop, become the master of your family's destiny. The debt will be yours to carry, and yours to discharge. Do you understand?"
Winthrop could only nod, his heart too full for words. Mr. Thorne was not just giving him money; he was giving him back his self-respect. He was turning this humiliating plea into a contract between men, a challenge that he could meet with work and time. He was exchanging a crushing, impossible burden for a heavy, but manageable one.
"It will be a long road," Mr. Thorne said, his voice softening again. "But you are young and strong. 'The wrestling of this worlde askith a fall', as your Chaucer says. But it also buildeth sinew and strength for the next bout. This is your fall, Winthrop. Now you will learn how to rise."
He went to a small writing-desk, drew out a cheque-book, and began to write. Winthrop watched him, the scratching of the pen the sweetest music he had ever heard. It was the sound of his home being saved, of his mother's tears being dried, of his father's shoulders being unburdened.
Mr. Thorne folded the draft and handed it to him. "Send this to your father. Tell him to pay the man and be free. We will settle the paperwork between us next week."
Winthrop took the slip of paper. He looked at the amount written there, and then at the kind, wise face of the man who had written it.
"Sir," he said, and his voice was clear and steady now, filled with an emotion deeper than gratitude. "I do not know how to thank you."
"Thank me by becoming the man I believe you to be," said Mr. Thorne. "Now go. Your sister will be wondering where you are."
Winthrop walked out of that house as if on air. The city streets, which had seemed so hostile an hour before, now shone with a brilliant light. He carried a heavy new debt, a responsibility that would shadow him for a decade, but his spirit felt light and free. He had faced his wilderness, and a path had been made.
He came back to the little attic room to find Winnie watching for him at the window. She ran to him as he entered.
"Oh, Governor, you were gone so long! I was afraid."
He swung her up in his arms, his face radiant. "There is nothing to be afraid of, my Winnie. Not anymore. The shadows are beginning to flee."
She looked at his transformed face, at the joy that shone in his eyes. She did not understand what had happened, but she understood that.
"You fixed it, didn't you, Governor?" she said, her trust absolute. "I knew you would."
He held her close, burying his face in her hair. "God has been very good to us, Winnie," he whispered.
Later that evening, he sat down to write to his father. He enclosed the precious draft, explaining the arrangement he had made. It was a letter full of hope and renewed strength, and as he sealed it, he felt not the weight of the great debt he had taken on, but the profound, quiet joy of a son who had, at last, been able to save his home.
